[1] The Ostler Grange hall had a stage two feet high and, on the first and third Saturdays of every month, a square dance that had been called for thirty-one years by Hollis Varga. By the winter I was fourteen, Hollis was seventy-nine, and his voice, which had once carried to the parking lot without a microphone, had begun to go thin by the second hour. My grandmother, who danced in the third square from the door told him at the coffee urn that he ought to train somebody. He looked around the hall, and I was the only person in it under forty.

[2] I thought I knew what I was agreeing to. I had been dancing since I was nine, and I knew the figures the way you know the rooms of your own house: allemande left, promenade, do-si-do. Calling, as far as I could see, was saying those words in order into a microphone, loudly and with some swagger. The swagger I planned to borrow from Hollis.

[3] He started me at a card table in his kitchen with eight salt and pepper shakers standing in for four couples. "Call it," he said, and I called a sequence I had danced a hundred times, and he moved the shakers exactly as I told them to move, and at the end the pepper that had started beside its salt was standing next to a stranger. I had not got them home. He set the shakers back without comment and said, "Again." It was the first of a great many agains.

[4] What I had not understood was that a call has to arrive before the music does. A square needs a beat to hear a call, another to work out what it means, and a third to start moving, so a caller who says "promenade" on the beat where the promenade should begin has already made eight people late. "You're not describing what they're doing," he said. "You're telling them what they're about to do. If you're on the beat, you're behind."

[5] The second thing took longer, and I did not learn it in the kitchen. In February he let me call one tip, a patter call and a singing call, on a night when two of the squares were mostly newcomers from the college. I had worked up a patter sequence around a figure, spin chain through, that I was proud of and that the regulars liked; I could see my grandmother's square take it and grin. By the second time through, the square nearest the stage had stopped dancing. Two couples were turned the wrong way, one of the newcomers had both hands raised as if somebody were robbing her, and the square stood still while the music went on without them.

[6] I did what I had planned, which was to keep calling. The other squares were fine. I called the sequence through again, louder, and the stopped square watched the others with the expressions of people at a bus stop watching their bus pull away. At the side of the stage, Hollis lifted one hand an inch off his knee and set it back down.

[7] On the third time through I dropped the spin chain. I don't remember deciding to; I remember the word not coming out. I called the dancers into lines, called a forward and back, the oldest and plainest figure there is, and then an allemande left, which every newcomer in that hall had learned in the first ten minutes of the evening. The stopped square found its corners. I called a promenade, and they promenaded, and I got all four squares home on the same phrase, which is the thing you want and which I had managed at the card table perhaps one time in five.

[8] Hollis did not tell me I had done well. In the car he said that my timing was still late on the singing call, and that spin chain through was a good figure for the first Saturday in May. I asked what was special about the first Saturday in May. "Nothing," he said. "But you'll know the floor by then."

[9] It was years before I understood him. A caller does not call to the best square in the hall, or to the one your grandmother is in. You call to the square that is about to break down, because a square that stops does not stand there for long; it goes and sits down, and the next month it does not come back. My grandmother's square would have danced to anything. That was exactly why it could not tell me whether I was calling well.

[1] Every language borrows. English took "coffee," probably by way of Dutch, from Turkish, which had taken it from Arabic. Japanese took pan, its everyday word for bread, from Portuguese traders in the sixteenth century. What languages differ in is how much they borrow and how quickly, and the question of why turns out to be harder than it looks.

[2] One of the most careful attempts to measure the difference, a comparative project published in 2009, examined about forty languages. For each one it checked roughly fifteen hundred basic meanings (body parts, family members, weather, tools, everyday actions) and asked how many were expressed by a borrowed word. The results ranged enormously. In a variety of Romani spoken in Slovakia, more than half the words on the list had been borrowed. English came in at around two in five, a high figure that reflects centuries of borrowing from Norse, French, and Latin. Mandarin Chinese came in at the bottom, with only one or two words in a hundred.

[3] The same project found that what gets borrowed is far from random. Nouns crossed over much more readily than verbs, and words for new things, such as foods, tools, and institutions, far more readily than words for the body or for close family. The meanings that resisted borrowing best were the ones every speaker uses every day from early childhood. When such everyday words do change hands, it is a sign of something more than trade. English "they," "them," and "their" came from Old Norse, during the centuries when Norse and English speakers lived side by side in northern and eastern England, married into each other's families, and raised children who heard both languages.

[4] That example points to the factor linguists usually name first: the kind of contact. Casual contact, through merchants, a few travelers, or books, tends to bring in words for the things being traded or written about, and little else. Long and intimate contact, in which many people are bilingual over generations, can bring in almost anything, including grammar. The Romani variety at the top of the list is spoken by a community whose members have for generations also spoken Hungarian and Slovak in daily life. Its high count is a record of that daily bilingualism, not of any weakness in the language.

[5] Contact cannot be the whole explanation, however, because languages in similar situations sometimes behave very differently. Here attitudes matter. For roughly two centuries, Icelandic speakers have preferred to build new words from old Icelandic parts rather than adopt foreign ones; the Icelandic word for "computer," tölva, joins the word for "number" to an old word for a prophetess. France has gone further and backed the preference with institutions: official bodies publish recommended French terms, and a 1994 law requires French in many kinds of public and commercial communication. Such efforts do not stop borrowing (French speakers say "le week-end" whatever the recommendations), but they slow it, and they show that a community's opinion of borrowing is itself a force acting on the result.

[6] A third factor is structural, and it is the one most often proposed for Mandarin's low figure. Mandarin syllables follow a narrow set of patterns, and in writing each syllable is represented by a character that carries a meaning of its own, so a word borrowed for its sound alone tends to read as a string of unrelated meanings. Mandarin has often preferred to translate the idea instead: a computer is commonly called diànnǎo, "electric brain." Japanese, by contrast, has a separate syllabic script, katakana, used largely for words of foreign origin, which lets a borrowed word be written by its sound without dragging any meanings along. Japanese borrows heavily, especially from English.

[7] It would be tidy to rank these three factors, but the evidence does not allow it, because they interact. Japanese had katakana for many centuries before its great wave of English borrowing, which followed the intensified contact of the twentieth century; the script made borrowing easy, but contact supplied the words. Attitudes, meanwhile, can shift faster than either contact or structure. A generation that finds foreign words fashionable can undo much of what an earlier generation's caution achieved.

[8] What the comparison does settle is a common misconception. A language that borrows heavily is not losing itself, and one that borrows little is not being more faithful. English, with roughly two-fifths of its basic vocabulary borrowed, is in no danger; Mandarin, with almost none, is in no better health. A language's borrowing rate is a record of whom its speakers have lived among and what they have thought of those neighbors: a history written in vocabulary, not a measure of strength.

passage_title: How Much a Label Should Say: Two Views
passage:
Passage A

[1] Three years ago, when our small museum reinstalled its gallery of nineteenth-century landscapes, I took most of the words off the walls. Each painting kept what museum staff call a tombstone label, which gives the artist's name, the title, the date, and the materials, and lost the paragraph beneath it. Some colleagues were alarmed, and a few visitors wrote to complain. Most visitors, as far as we could tell, did not notice the change at all, and that was close to the point.

[2] Anyone who has watched people in a gallery knows the pattern. A visitor arrives in front of a picture, glances at it, finds the label, reads the label, glances at the picture again as if to check that the label was accurate, and moves on. Studies of museum visitors have repeatedly found that people spend well under a minute at a typical work, and in our galleries a good share of that minute was going to the wall beside the painting. The label had become the object, and the painting its illustration.

[3] I do not think information is bad for looking. I think it is bad for looking when it arrives first. A paragraph announcing that a sky is "luminous" decides what you will see before you have seen it, and a visitor who reads that the painter admired some famous predecessor goes looking for the influence rather than for the painting. The words close questions the visitor has not yet had time to open. Better that the visitor stand before the sky long enough to decide what it is doing, and only then read what others have thought.

[4] So we moved the information rather than abolishing it. The longer texts are now in a booklet at the gallery entrance and in a reading room at the end, where a visitor who has looked can find out what was in front of them. When we timed visitors before and after the change, the average time spent in front of each painting rose noticeably. I would not claim the numbers prove that people saw more. But they were, at least, looking at the paintings rather than at the walls.

Passage B

[1] The short label is usually defended as the modest choice, the one that steps aside and lets the work speak. It is nothing of the kind. Every line of a tombstone label is an argument with its reasoning removed.

[2] Take the artist's name. Many older paintings were not made by a single hand, and museums have a careful vocabulary for saying so: "attributed to," "workshop of," "follower of." Each phrase records a judgment, often a disputed one, made by particular scholars at a particular time, yet printed in small capitals without comment it looks like a fact. The title is frequently no better. Many older pictures were named not by their painters but by later dealers or cataloguers, and a title such as Peaceful Evening instructs the eye as firmly as any paragraph about a luminous sky.

[3] The trouble with the old long labels was not their length. It was that they answered questions nobody in the gallery was asking, such as where the painter trained or which movement the painting belongs to, in the voice of an authority that could not be doubted. A label could instead tell visitors what is not known: that the attribution was changed in 1974 and may change again, that the title is a dealer's, that the bright patch in one corner is a later repair. Information of that kind does not close questions. It hands visitors the questions the experts are still arguing about.

[4] Visitors given only a name and a date are not left free to see for themselves. They are left to accept, without knowing it, a set of decisions that someone else made and chose not to show them. A wall stripped to its tombstone has not removed the museum's voice from the room. It has only made that voice quieter, and harder to argue with.
